Maladaptive Strategies.value: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a trauma type of trauma to a loved one, the appraisal that the patient's own body has been permanently damaged is hard to reconcile unless the patient also directly sustained major physical injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoidance of medical cues can fit some trauma-to-a-loved-one cases, but in this profile it appears to be driven by a personal bodily injury/medical trauma theme that is otherwise unsupported except by the implausible physical-vulnerability appraisal, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the profile.

vignette: Two years ago, during the October parish harvest, Clara, married to Thomas for thirty years, had turned away to adjust the heavy donation box. She trusted he would remain seated on the stone bench beyond the refectory, but when she looked back, he was on the ground, his wool coat splayed against the pavers, his hands caught in the exact position she remembered. The moment arrived with sudden clarity. The way his collar had twisted, the sharp sound of the stone, the sudden hush beneath the crowd's noise are etched in her mind like glass, while the seconds after he hit the ground are a quiet void. Some moments are crystal clear; others are completely blank. She had come to believe the event unfolded the way she remembered it. She was certain that her brief departure left him unguarded, and she carried a quiet self-blame for the gap in her attention. What frightened her most was the realization that she could not rely on herself to read the room, to anticipate the sudden drop, to be steady enough in the moment. The memory of his fall sits beside a steady doubt: she should have protected him, and somewhere in the blur of stone and voices, she had failed to do so. On most days, Clara passes the courtyard without pausing, but the past several months have brought sudden shifts. A gust of wind off the alley stirred the same dry leaves that rustled that afternoon, and the full scene arrived without warning. A dropped rosary or the scent of damp wool from the laundry room pulls the memory forward instantly, while at other times, the event recedes into a soft stillness. Over the weeks, she developed quiet habits. She began taking the side gate to the courtyard, walking the long perimeter so she never crossed the exact stones where he fell. She found herself avoiding the parish gift shop, where a familiar scarf caught her eye and reminded her of the seasons to come. When the weight of the past rose, she performed mental rituals: counting the steps to the chapel door, silently repeating the litany of the saints, mentally verifying that the stove was off and the windows latched. These gestures did not quiet the memories, but they gave her a way to hold them. Her work as a nun frames these days. The courtyard's proximity to the refectory and the scripture room means her avoidance is woven into her routine. The sisters have noticed that Clara now schedules her morning duties around the side entrance, and she has taken to organizing the parish archives, keeping her hands busy with ledgers and paper that do not require her to look out the windows. The consequence has been quiet but steady: she has stepped back from leading the weekly community prayer, finding the open space of the nave too vast, too exposed, when the wind moves through the glass. The accumulated weight of these habits brought her to the clinic. She is fifty-five now, and she comes each Tuesday with a small notebook of things she cannot quite trust herself to remember. Her PCL5 score of 42 mirrored these quiet days. What she is most hoping for is a way to walk through the gate without counting every stone, to stand in the nave without bracing, and to accept that her care for him was enough, even when the memory does not arrive with full clarity.
